name: Sari
confidence_why: Langhout 2012 and 2015 describe Sari with three level tonemes and grammatical tone and put stress on the stem-initial syllable, and Richards 1991 independently treats stress as phonologically distinctive alongside tone in Sali, Noone and Ncanti, so the tonal reading is unopposed but rests on only two independent descriptions, one of them known only from its abstract.
catalog_citation: Langhout, Bep. 2015. Grammar Sketch of the Sari Language: Noun Classes. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 55 pp. (open PDF)
catalog_locator: pp. 4-5, section 2.1 Phonemes: [ɾ]-allophone remark p. 4; consonant phoneme/allophone/grapheme chart rows /l/ [l] 'filoŋ' and [ɾ] 'nduru', footnotes 2 and 3; tone: p. 8, section 2.3
catalog_quote: Contrary to what is presented in the phonology, I found that [ɾ] is an allophone of [l], with personal variation between the intervocalic [l] and [ɾ]. It will still be written as r. ... /l/ [l] Ll la filoŋ2 ___ / compound story / [ɾ] Rr nduru3 / corn ... 2 Stem-initial, stressed, giving [l] between vowels 3 Not stem-initial, not stressed, giving [ɾ] between vowels ... 2.3 Writing words with grammatical tone / In the Sari orthography tone is not written. In order to distinguish between certain grammatical forms that only differ in tone melody, there are at the moment three distinctions that are worth noting: the difference between singular and plural for nouns of noun gender 9/10, and the difference between a verb form in 1st person singular and 3rd person singular. ... The singular and plural forms from nouns in gender 9/10 differ only in tone. For instance (1) [nsɔ̀] 'leather drum', class 9 [nsɔ̄] 'leather drums', class 10

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata gives the title '151202.Sari.Noun classes.Final.BL', author Bep Langhout, 55 pp.). extracted text of PDF page 11 (printed p. 5, section 2.1 Phonemes, consonant phoneme/allophone/grapheme chart) shows the row '/l/ [l] Ll la filoŋ2 ___ / compound story' and '[ɾ] Rr nduru3 / corn', and at the foot of the page the footnotes exactly as quoted: '2 Stem-initial, stressed, giving [l] between vowels' and '3 Not stem-initial, not stressed, giving [ɾ] between vowels'. Verbatim. Surrounding section (pp. 4-8): 'The phonology is described in Julius A. Eyoh (2007). Below a summary is given'; 'Contrary to what is presented in the phonology, I found that [ɾ] is an allophone of [l]…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sari is a three-tone language (H, M, L plus eight contour melodies; Orthography Guide 2022: 16). The only statement about stress is a footnote in Langhout's noun-class sketch: the stem-initial (root-initial) syllable is stressed and non-stem-initial syllables are unstressed; this stress conditions the allophony of /l/ ([l] when stem-initial/stressed, [ɾ] intervocalically elsewhere). Read as prominence on the first syllable of the root, i.e. after noun-class prefixes — a morphologically determined placement — but it is a passing remark, not a phonological analysis of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Langhout notes personal variation in the [l]~[ɾ] realisation ('Especially older women will say [l]', Orthography Guide 2022: 5 fn. 3). The 2022 orthography guide restates the same rule without the word 'stressed' ('The /l/ at the start of a root is pronounced [l].. The /l/ between vowels at other places is pronounced [ɾ] or [l]').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, stem/root domain: the contrast is between the stem-initial syllable and later syllables of the word (noun-class prefixes such as fi-, bi- precede the stem). Based on elicited words and texts in the Sari orthography. For the sister language Nchane, Boutwell (2020: 39-40) likewise notes root-initial intensity prominence and states that 'stress as a feature of the sound system has not been studied beyond the observances made here'.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Sari of Misaje Subdivision (villages Akweto, Kamine, Mbissa) = Glottolog nsar1238 / ISO asj. Langhout (2015, 2022) reports no major dialects, only personal speech variants in vowel length and tone. Richards 1991 calls the language 'Sali'; Hombert 1980 and Langhout 2012 spell it 'Saari'. Boutwell 2020 is about the sister language Nchane (ncan1245) and is cited here only for context.

new_statements.quote: Une attention toute particuliere est portee au role joue par l'accent, en rapport avec la fonction du ton et la distribution des differents types d'unites consonantiques et vocaliques constituant les schemes syllabiques. [...] ces schemes sont alors classes selon la place de l'accent. [...] Elle permet aussi de rendre compte des restrictions distributionnelles et combinatoires observees au niveau des tons modules et des unites complexes (consonnes prenasalisees, labialisees ou palatalisees ; voyelles longues ou nasales), qui n'apparaissent generalement qu'en syllabe accentuee. Ces restrictions ne pourraient pas s'expliquer de maniere non-arbitraire et satisfaisante si l'accent etait considere comme un trait non-pertinent au niveau de la phonologie.
new_statements.translation: Particular attention is paid to the role played by stress, in relation to the function of tone and the distribution of the different types of consonantal and vocalic units that make up the syllable patterns. [...] these patterns are then classified according to the place of the stress. [...] It also accounts for the distributional and combinatory restrictions observed on contour tones and complex units (prenasalized, labialized or palatalized consonants; long or nasal vowels), which generally appear only in stressed syllables. These restrictions could not be explained in a non-arbitrary and satisfactory way if stress were treated as a non-distinctive feature at the phonological level. (The parallel English abstract in the same record: 'SPECIAL CONSIDERATION IS GIVEN TO THE ROLE PLAYED BY STRESS AS IT RELATES TO TONE ... THESE PATTERNS ARE THEN CLASSIFIED ACCORDING TO STRESS PLACEMENT ... WHICH GENERALLY OCCUR ONLY IN STRESSED SYLLABLES.')

The French abstract contains every quoted sentence verbatim, including the unaccented spellings ('Une attention toute particuliere est portee au role joue par l'accent, en rapport avec la fonction du ton et la distribution des differents types d'unites consonantiques et vocaliques constituant les schemes syllabiques'.. Ces restrictions ne pourraient pas s'expliquer de maniere non-arbitraire et satisfaisante si l'accent etait…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Langhout 2015 statement (stem-initial syllable stressed, conditioning [l] vs [ɾ]): Richards' abstract adds that stress is phonologically distinctive and that complex segments and contour tones are confined to stressed syllables, but gives no placement rule. It also covers Noone and Ncanti (sister languages), so the claim is for the group, not Sari alone. Abstract-only evidence: the thesis body could not be opened.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the three Eastern Beboid languages treated (Noone, Ncanti, Sali = Sari), the thesis abstract says stress is a phonologically distinctive feature alongside tone: syllable patterns are classified by stress placement, and complex segments (prenasalized/labialized/palatalized consonants, long or nasal vowels) and contour tones are generally restricted to stressed syllables. The abstract does not state where the stress falls; the body of the thesis (which presumably does) is not accessible online.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; 'generally' (généralement) qualifies the restriction of complex units to stressed syllables
new_statements.identity_note: Langhout 2012 describes the Saari of Akweto/Kamine (Besaa people, between Nkambe and Misaje, Donga-Mantung), with all tone data from a single speaker (Wilson Nformi, parents from Bakinchine); it names Akweto, Nsari, Pesaa, Sali as alternate names. Richards 1991 treats 'Sali' (= Sari, nsar1238) together with Noone (Noni) and Ncanti (Nchane), and its abstract makes its stress claim for the three languages jointly.

readall_conflicts: No direct disagreement on placement. One minor tension in the evidence base: the catalog's only placement statement (Langhout 2015, footnotes to the consonant chart: stem-initial = stressed, giving [l]; non-stem-initial = unstressed, giving [ɾ]) is not repeated in Langhout 2012, which explains the same [l]~[ɾ] alternation as personal variation with no reference to stress. Richards 1991 (abstract only) asserts that stress is phonologically distinctive in Noone, Ncanti and Sali and that complex segments and contour tones are generally confined to stressed syllables, but the abstract gives no placement rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the stem-initial placement. Boutwell 2020 (Nchane, sister language, held by the project from an earlier reading, not in the works list) similarly notes root-initial position as 'associated with stress (as indicated by an apparent increase in intensity)' while saying stress 'has not been studied beyond the observances made here' — consistent with a root-initial prominence pattern in the group, but not about Sari.
